routes.speaker: Keith Ward
routes.description: Ward supports God's existence by arguing that experience, intelligibility, morality, and mind point beyond appearances to a mind-like spiritual reality, while limiting the divine attributes his case requires.

bridges.description: Establish that a mind-like spiritual reality reasonably identified as God exists.
Show that reality beneath sensory appearances is fundamentally mind-like rather than exhaustively physical.
Connect the universe's rational and mathematical intelligibility to an underlying intelligence.
Connect objective moral demand and universal compassion to the spiritual reality Ward calls God.
Defend transcendent experience as genuine access to more than sensory and physical reality.

routes.speaker: Stephen Law
routes.description: Law argues that familiar explanatory arguments do not establish a good God, suffering and evil-God symmetry count strongly against that hypothesis, and human unreliability about hidden agents defeats experiential warrant.

bridges.description: Establish that the available evidence does not warrant belief that God exists.
Show that cosmological, design, and intelligibility considerations do not identify a divine or morally good creator.
Show that extensive apparently gratuitous suffering is evidence against a supremely powerful and benevolent God.
Use symmetry with an evil-God hypothesis to test whether standard arguments and theodicies support a good God.
Show that known human over-detection of hidden agency defeats reliance on subjective religious experience.

sections.title: Mind-like reality beyond appearance
sections.rationale: This exchange tests whether the gap between appearances and underlying reality supports a mind-like ontology or merely leaves hypotheses open.

sections.title: Intelligibility and cosmic explanation
sections.rationale: This section collects the proposed inference from rational structure to intelligence and the rival-explanation challenge to design reasoning.

sections.title: Divine goodness and suffering
sections.rationale: The central dispute is whether Ward's moral conception of God survives Law's evidential case from extensive suffering.

sections.title: Evil-God symmetry and theodicy
sections.rationale: Law uses an evil-God analogue to pressure both positive arguments and standard explanations of suffering; Ward answers by weakening omnipotence and stressing lawful destructive conditions.

sections.title: Religious experience and hidden agency
sections.rationale: This section tests Ward's experiential route against Law's epistemic defeater from systematic false hidden-agent beliefs.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: The evil-God section is source-asymmetric because Law presents four distinct load-bearing moves: cosmic-argument symmetry, observational good/evil symmetry, a mirrored free-will defense, and a mirrored stable-laws defense. Ward's single selected answer there is his distinct necessity claim about destructive lawful conditions; his separate rejection of omnipotence belongs in the divine-goodness section. None of Law's four moves is a duplicate or a placeholder, and merging them would erase independently assessable warrants. The debate-wide selection remains nearly balanced at nine Ward moves and ten Law moves.

sections.rationale: The asymmetric fourth row is preauthorized because Law's four independently warranted and non-mergeable moves test different evidence and defenses within one coherent evil-God symmetry exchange; Ward has one distinct directly relevant reply and no counterpart is manufactured.

audit.speakerAttributionBasis: Opening speakers are fixed by the participant-host invitation and source-lock windows; direct-interaction turns are explicitly handed between Ward and Law; Q&A answers are attributed from the addressee and continuity with each participant's distinctive first-person case. Audience questions and participant-host logistics are not selected as moves.
